name: Thiripuranthakeswarar Temple, Koovam (Thiruvirkolam)
deity: Shiva as Thiripuranthakeswarar, destroyer of the three cities, with the Goddess Thiripuranthaki (Tripurasundari)
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, sung in the Tevaram by Sambandar (7th century)
dynasty: Thondai Nadu, with Chola-period records and later rebuilding
summary: At Koovam, where the river of that name is said to rise, Shiva stands as the archer who destroyed the three flying cities — Thiruvirkolam, the sacred form with the bow, sung by Sambandar.

sections.history: Koovam is a village in Tiruvallur district, west of Chennai near Perambakkam, and its old name in the hymns is Thiruvirkolam — the place of the Lord's sacred form with the bow. It is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams, a Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, sung by Sambandar in a pathigam of the Tevaram. The village gives its name to the Koovam river, which tradition says rises here, and the bond is kept in worship: water from the river is brought for the Lord's ablution. Chola-period records of the village speak of its great tank and of the temple's part in caring for it.
sections.architecture: The temple is a Dravidian shrine of the northern Tamil plain, with the sanctum of Thiripuranthakeswarar and a separate shrine for the Goddess Thiripuranthaki. The lingam is held to be self-manifested, and it is honoured as the Theenda Thirumeni — the sacred form that is not touched, even by the priests. Devotees speak of its colour seeming to change with the seasons. A shrine of Vinayaka recalls the temple's legend, and two tanks, the Agni Theertham and the Kopagni Theertham, belong to the shrine.
sections.legends: When Shiva rode out to destroy the three flying cities of the asuras, the gods who made his chariot set out without first honouring Vinayaka. On the way the axle broke. Only when the gods turned back and worshipped the remover of obstacles did the journey go on — and here, the sthala purana says, the Lord appeared armed with his bow, giving the place its name. The Vinayaka of the shrine is remembered as the one who broke the axle, and devotees pray to him before beginning any new undertaking.
sections.festivals: Pradosham and Maha Shivaratri are kept with special worship, with Karthigai Deepam and the temple's annual festival of the Lord. Vinayaka Chaturthi has a particular place here because of the shrine's legend; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Koovam is a quiet village temple, and its customs are its own: devotees honour the Goddess before the Lord, and couples come to pray for harmony in marriage. The priests begin their day with a dip in the Agni Theertham, a tank held never to run dry. Pilgrims stop first at the shrine of Vinayaka, as the legend teaches, before standing before the archer-lord whom no hand may touch.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Koovam lies in Tiruvallur district, near Perambakkam and Kadambathur, and is reached by road from Tiruvallur, Sriperumbudur or Chennai. Tiruvallur and Kadambathur are stations on the Chennai–Arakkonam suburban line; Chennai International Airport is the nearest airport.
